newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says NATO enlargement "an evolving process".
newsitem.headline: France says NATO enlargement "an evolving process".

text.p: France, acknowledging that it will not budge the United States from limiting the first wave of ex-communist countries admitted to NATO to three, said on Friday the enlargement of the alliance would be an evolving process.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said Paris considered that five countries were fit to join now and in the long term, all European countries which shared the Atlantic alliance's values had a right to NATO membership.
"The enlargement of NATO will be an evolving process," Rummelhardt told a routine briefing.
"We consider that at the moment five countries have a right to be members of the Atlantic alliance. We are also in favour of the accession of the three which the Americans also support," he said.

U.S. President Bill Clinton reaffirmed on Thursday that only the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland were politically and militarily qualified to be invited to join NATO by a summit of the 16-nation defence alliance in Madrid next week.

"I don't want to exclude anyone, but I think it quite important on principle that we not admit anyone until we're absolutely sure that their democracy is stable and that they are militarily capable," Clinton said in an interview with European television stations.
France has campaigned for Romania and Slovenia to be added to the first group.
Rummelhardt made his remarks in briefing reporters on the visit of Lithuanian President Algirdas Brazauskas to Paris from next week.
The implication of his comment was that France considered that Lithuania and other Baltic states too would eventually be entitled to NATO membership.

Russia has adamantly opposed the admission of any former Soviet republics to the western military alliance, warning that such a move would force it to reconsider the "Founding Act" on a cooperative relationship it signed with NATO in May.

Western leaders have said Moscow cannot have a veto over who joins the alliance, but officials say there is no prospect of NATO admitting the Baltic republics in the forseeable future and their best hope is eventual European Union membership.
